title: Why Payments Fail: How Businesses in Southeast Asia Can Reduce and Recover Failed Payments
summary: Learn why payments fail, which failures your business can recover, and how to turn more declined payments into completed revenue across Southeast Asia. The post Why Payments Fail: How Businesses in Southeast Asia Can Reduce and Recover Failed Payments appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
A


**failed payment** is any payment attempt that ends without a completed transaction, whether the issuing bank declines it, the customer abandons authentication, or a system error interrupts it along the way.


Because each of these outcomes has a different cause, your business gains the most by asking three questions about every failure: why it happened, whether it can still be recovered, and what path the customer can take to complete the purchase.


Some payment attempts may not go through, even when your checkout and payment setup are working as intended. Understanding why payments fail affects how many of those failed attempts your business can still turn into completed transactions.


**Here is what this article covers:**


- The common reasons why payments fail, and why each one needs its own response


- Which metrics show where payments fail and whether those failures can be recovered


- How to match retries, alternative payment methods, and customer guidance to each failure reason


- How Xendit's decline data, recovery features, and real-time payment status help your team act on each failed payment


- How VCGamers and a global wellness platform raised their payment success rates


## **Common reasons why payments fail at scale**


Payments can fail for many different reasons, and for businesses operating across Southeast Asia, payment success also changes by market, payment method, card type, issuing bank, and the context of each transaction.


A payment marked as failed in your system can describe very different situations. When transaction volume is low, your team may be able to review and resolve failed payments one by one. Once


**the number of failed payments grows** , reviewing each case manually is no longer practical, so your business needs to identify the type of each failure first and apply the right response.


These


**patterns** explain


**why payment failures become harder to manage** as transaction volume grows:


- **Different payment failures require different responses** The same failed status can come from causes that have nothing in common. Here is how


**common failure reasons lead to different actions** for your team:


- **Insufficient funds** The customer's account or card does not have enough balance or credit to cover the payment. \\


- **Expired or incorrect card details** The saved card has passed its expiry date, or the customer entered the card number, expiry date, or CVN incorrectly.


- **An issuer risk decision** The issuing bank declined the payment because the payment matched the bank's risk rules, for example an unusual amount, location, or merchant category.


- **A temporary processor or issuer issue** A system at the issuing bank, card network, or payment processor was briefly unavailable or took too long to respond.


- **Many payment failures happen after the payment leaves your checkout** Card payments may be declined by issuing banks, while e-wallet payments can fail due to expired requests or channel issues. Xendit helps merchants identify the most probable card decline reasons.


- **Cross-border transactions add another layer of decline risk** Cross-border payments can fail despite sufficient funds due to issuer rules, authentication requirements, or geographic restrictions. These declines may require different recovery strategies from domestic transactions.

## **Key payment metrics to track before reducing failed payments**


Your business needs to know where payments fail, why they fail, and whether those failures can be recovered. This starts with an accurate view of the stage in the payment process where each failure happens, whether at checkout, during authentication, at the issuing bank, or at the payment channel.


**Tracking the following payment metrics** shows your team where payments fail and which failures to fix first:


### **Authorization rate**


Authorization rate is the


**percentage of payment attempts** that end in a


**successful** ,


**approved** transaction. To calculate authorization rate,


[divide successful transactions by total transaction attempts and multiply by 100](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/how-to-reduce-failed-payments-and-improve-authorization-rates/) .


For example, if your business processes 20,000 payment attempts in a month and 18,400 of them are approved, your authorization rate is 92%.


A count of failed payments can be misleading, because the count rises whenever total volume rises. If your business processes twice as many payments in one month, the number of failed payments may also double even though the share of failed payments stays the same.


Authorization rate shows that share as a percentage, so your team can tell whether payment performance is actually improving or declining. For your business, tracking authorization rate every month shows whether changes to your payment setup are working.


### **Payment failure rate by reason, method, and market**


Overall failure rate shows how many payments fail, but does not show which part of your payment setup causes those failures. To find the cause, break payment failures down into the following categories:


**Decline reason**


Grouping failures by reason, such as insufficient funds, expired cards, or issuer risk rules, shows which causes accounts for the most lost transactions and which fix will recover the most revenue.


**Payment method**


Comparing cards, e-wallets, bank transfers, QR payments, and your other methods shows whether one method fails more often, for example an e-wallet whose payment requests often expire before customers complete them.


**Geography**


Looking at each market separately shows whether customers in one country experience more failed payments than customers elsewhere in the region.


**Card type**


Separating credit, debit, and prepaid cards shows whether one card type is declined more often, for example because of daily spending limits on debit cards.


**Issuing bank**


Tracking declines by issuer shows whether one bank declines far more payments than others, which can point to that bank's risk rules or a technical issue on the bank's side.


**Transaction context**


Comparing first-time and repeat purchases, domestic and cross-border payments, or low and high order values shows which situations lead issuers to apply extra checks.


Authorization rates differ by payment method, market, and decline reason. Your overall rate can look healthy even when payments from one country or one issuing bank fail much more often than the rest. Reviewing each category separately helps your team


**find those weak spots** and


**fix the ones that will recover the most transactions** .


### **Retry success rate**


If your business retries failed payments, retry success rate shows how many of those retries eventually succeed. It


**separates** payment


**failures that recover with time** , such as a temporary issuer outage or a customer topping up their balance, from


**failures that need the customer to act** , such as updating card details.


For your business, a low retry success rate for one type of decline, such as expired cards, shows that automatic retries are not working for that group of payments. Your team can stop retrying those payments automatically and send the customers a different next step, such as a request to update their card details.


### **Effective cost per successful transaction**


Failed payments can still generate processing costs. Effective cost per successful transaction


**divides your total payment fees** , including fees charged on failed attempts,


**by the number of successful transactions** .


This figure gives your finance team the real cost of each completed payment, and it shows how much a higher authorization rate saves on top of the revenue it recovers.


***Also read:***[How Payment Success Rates Turn Checkout Demand Into E-Commerce Revenue](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/how-payment-success-rates-turn-checkout-demand-into-e-commerce-revenue/)


Once your team knows which failures happen most often and why, the next step is choosing the right recovery method for each type of failure.


## **How businesses can reduce and recover failed payments**


Different failure reasons need


**different recovery steps** . When every failed payment is retried in the same way, your business pays processing fees on attempts that cannot succeed, while payments that need action from the customer remain unrecovered.


To


**reduce failed payments** and recover more of the payments, your business can apply the following practices:


### **1. Match the response to the failure reason**


Not every failed payment should be retried. Depending on the decline reason, your system should take one of the following actions:


- Ask the customer to update their payment details


- Wait for a set interval before retrying


- Ask the customer to contact their bank


- Offer the customer another payment method


- Take no further action


[Mastercard merchant advice codes](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-card-declines-and-error-codes) tell your system which of these applies, including specific retry intervals that range from 1 hour to 10 days and cases where retrying is discouraged altogether. Following them matters for cost as well as recovery, because Mastercard can charge excessive retry fines of up to USD 0.50 per transaction when merchants keep retrying payments marked as do not retry.


For your business, building these rules into your retry logic cuts wasted attempts and focuses retries on the payments most likely to succeed.


### **2. Offer alternative payment methods as a fallback**


When a customer's card cannot complete the transaction, another payment method gives them a second path to purchase. This carries extra weight in Southeast Asia, where many customers keep their money in e-wallets and bank accounts and reach for those methods more often than cards.


A customer declined on a card for reaching the credit limit can often finish the same order through a bank transfer, a virtual account, or an e-wallet they already prefer to use. Broader payment method coverage gives customers


[fallback options when a card payment fails](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/how-to-reduce-failed-payments-and-improve-authorization-rates/) , and your business keeps the sale even when the card decline itself cannot be reversed.


### **3. Automate recovery for recurring payments**


Recurring payments run without the customer present, so a failed charge can go unnoticed until the subscription lapses. Automation lets your business retry eligible payments on a schedule without anyone handling each failed transaction manually.


Effective automation for recurring billing combines the following elements:


- Retries timed around when customers usually top up their accounts


- A backup payment channel that the system can charge when the primary one fails


- A manual payment option the customer can use to settle a failed cycle


[Xendit Subscriptions](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/subscriptions/) supports all three elements, so failed renewals can be retried, moved to a backup channel, or settled by the customer without your team handling each one manually.


***Also read:***[Cutting Involuntary Churn from Failed Payments for SaaS Businesses in Southeast Asia](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/cutting-involuntary-churn-from-failed-payments-for-saas-businesses-in-southeast-asia/)


### **4. Give customers a clear next step**


A failed payment should never leave the customer guessing what to do. Depending on the failure, your checkout page or payment notification should point the customer to one of these four next steps:


- Update their payment information


- Try the payment again later


- Contact their bank to approve the transaction


- Choose another payment method


The wording of these notifications is also important. We suggest not


[telling customers that their card verification number (CVN) was invalid](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-card-declines-and-error-codes) , because that detail can help fraudsters who are testing stolen card numbers. A general prompt to check card details or try another method protects both the customer and your business.


***Also read:[Managing Fraud Risk Across Southeast Asia: What Businesses Need to Know](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/managing-fraud-risk-across-southeast-asia-what-businesses-need-to-know/)***


Clear guidance turns a failed attempt into a transaction the customer can still complete. Applying these practices consistently across a large volume of transactions depends on the payment data and tools your payment provider makes available.


## **Improve your payment success rates with Xendit**


Detailed decline data lets your team set retry rules based on the actual reason behind each failure. Real-time payment status lets recovery steps start as soon as a payment fails, while the customer is still engaged with the purchase.


Xendit supports


**payment recovery** for businesses across Southeast Asia in the following ways:


### **Decline Insights in the Xendit Dashboard**


Xendit's estimate for each card decline appears in the


[Decline Insights](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-card-declines-and-error-codes) section of the Card Transaction Details page in


[your dashboard](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/your-dashboard) . Your operations and support teams can open any declined card transaction and see the likely cause without first asking the customer to call their bank.


That gives your team enough information to decide whether a transaction should be retried, redirected to another payment method, or handled through the customer's bank.


### **Network response codes and merchant advice codes in card responses**


Xendit returns card network data together with Xendit failure codes in the authorization data of each card payment. The data includes the


[network response code](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-card-declines-and-error-codes) and its description from Visa, Mastercard, JCB, China UnionPay, or American Express, plus the Mastercard merchant advice code and its description whenever Mastercard provides one. For example, a response can tell your system that a payment exceeded the card's withdrawal count limit and should be retried after 6 days.


Your engineers can receive this data through webhooks or


[retrieve the same data through the Payments API](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/retrieving-authorization-and-decline-details) . With these details mapped into your retry logic, your system can sort each declined payment into retry now, retry later, route to another method, or stop.


### **3DS2 authentication details for failed card authentications**


Many cross-border card failures happen during


[3D Secure 2 (3DS2) authentication](https://docs.xendit.co/v1/docs/authentication-3ds2) , the extra verification step where the issuing bank confirms the cardholder's identity. The bank can verify the customer in the background, known as a frictionless flow, or ask the customer to verify the payment directly, for example through their banking app, known as a challenge.


Xendit passes through the 3DS2 authentication status and the flow the customer went through, and when authentication fails, the issuer's reason code and the challenge cancel code.


### **Multiple payment methods through one integration**


Xendit gives your business access to


[more than 100 payment methods](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/all-payment-methods/) across Southeast Asia, including cards, e-wallets, virtual accounts, direct debit, QR payments, and over-the-counter channels, through one integration. Your team can


[activate additional payment channels](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/activate-payment-channels) from the Xendit Dashboard when a market needs another fallback option.


Each payment channel has its own


[minimum and maximum transaction amount and payment request expiry time](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) , so your checkout can show only the methods that fit each order value. A customer declined on a card can then finish the order through another supported method, and an order above one channel's limit can be directed to a channel that accepts it before the payment fails.


### **Payment recovery for recurring transactions**


[Xendit Subscriptions](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/subscriptions-overview) lets your business attach up to five payment channels to each subscriber's plan and set the order in which they are charged. When the first channel fails, Xendit automatically tries the next one, following the retry interval, number of retries, and customer notifications set when the plan was created. Webhooks report whether each cycle succeeded, failed, or is still in retries.


For each failed attempt, Xendit can also send the customer a one-time


[Payment Link](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/payment-links/) to


[settle that cycle](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/recover-failed-payments) with any payment method, including one not attached to the plan. Businesses that run their own billing engine can


[store customer cards as tokens](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-recurring-and-merchant-initiated-transactions) through the Payments API, which helps reduce failures caused by expired or updated card details. For your business, each renewal gets several routes to succeed before it turns into involuntary churn.


### **Real-time payment status through webhooks and the Payments API**


The


[Get Payment endpoint](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/get-payment) of Xendit's Payments API returns the current status of any payment, such as pending, authorized, succeeded, failed, expired, or canceled, along with a failure code when the payment does not complete.


[Payments API webhooks](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/payments-api-webhooks) notify your systems as events happen, for example when a payment is captured or authorized, when a payment fails or expires, or when a payment request expires before the customer pays.


Xendit also sends a payment token expiry event when a saved card passes its expiry date, which gives your team an early warning before the next scheduled charge fails. With these events feeding your systems, your business can trigger the right next step automatically, whether that means releasing an order, sending a Payment Link, or asking a customer to update a saved card.

### **A global wellness platform: 198% higher international card success rates**


A Bali-founded wellness platform offers yoga teacher training, retreats, and community programs to students from more than 100 countries. Program fees usually range from USD 1,000 to 1,500, and most students enroll with international credit or debit cards.


The platform wanted to raise the


**approval rate for US and Canadian cards** , which was below 30%. Issuing banks applied strict verification rules, inconsistent or missing payment details led to declines, and the high transaction values often triggered extra scrutiny on the first attempt.


Xendit worked on three areas with the platform:


- **Checkout data quality:** Xendit optimized the checkout so payment details were captured in the format international issuers expect to verify.


- **Payment network alignment:** Xendit worked with banking partners to categorize the platform's payments correctly for retreats, wellness, and education, which reduced unnecessary declines.


- **Retry guidance:** On-screen prompts advised students to contact their bank and retry when a large payment was flagged on the first attempt.


[International card success rates rose to between 60% and 80%](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/wellness-platform/) , a


**198% improvement** . The retry prompts contributed directly, with students who contacted their bank and retried seeing


**approval rates rise by up to 15%** .


**Takeaway:** A failed payment does not always mean the customer lacks funds or a system has broken. Cross-border and high-value payments often recover through better payment data, correct transaction classification, and clear guidance for the customer.


Any business processing payments through Xendit can use the same tools to recover more failed payments as transaction volume grows.

Failed payments are part of processing transactions at scale, and their impact is something your business can manage. From there, your business can combine clearer visibility, well-timed retries, alternative payment methods, and simple recovery paths for customers to turn more failed attempts into completed transactions. ## **FAQ for businesses in Southeast Asia: Failed payments and payment recovery**


**What does a "do not honor" card decline mean?**


"Do not honor" is


[network response code 05](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-card-declines-and-error-codes) , which issuers often use when they do not trust a transaction or have not mapped a more specific reason. The recommended action is for the customer to try a different card, since retrying the same card rarely changes the issuer's decision.


**Xendit** groups this code under the declined by issuer failure reason and shows an estimate of the underlying cause in


[Decline Insights](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-card-declines-and-error-codes) , so your team can decide between asking for another card and offering a different payment method.


**Why do international card payments get declined when the customer has enough funds?**


Cross-border card payments often fail on issuer rules and authentication requirements, even when the balance is sufficient.


[Network response code 62](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-card-declines-and-error-codes) means the card is restricted and not valid in the merchant's country or region, while Visa's code 1A means the transaction needs authentication and can be retried with


[3DS2 authentication](https://docs.xendit.co/v1/docs/authentication-3ds2) .


**Xendit** returns both codes in the card response, which tells your team whether to ask for a different card or send the customer back through authentication.


**How can I tell if a failed payment came from the issuer or from my own integration?**


The failure code shows where the payment stopped. Failure codes such as declined by issuer, insufficient balance, or expired card point to the customer's bank or card, while processor error, invalid merchant settings, or network response code 03 (invalid merchant) point to processing or configuration issues to raise with Xendit.


**Xendit** returns the failure code for each payment through the


[Get Payment endpoint](https://docs.xendit.co/apidocs/get-payment) and publishes the full list of


[failure codes and error scenarios](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/simulate-error-scenarios) , so your engineers can test how your system handles each one before going live.


**Why are prepaid cards declined for subscription payments?**


Some issuers do not allow recurring charges on prepaid cards, so the renewal fails even when the balance covers the amount.


[Network response codes 39 and 57](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-card-declines-and-error-codes) can indicate that a card is not suitable for this type of transaction, and the recommended action is to use a different card.


**Xendit** returns these codes in the card response, and


[Xendit Subscriptions](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/subscriptions-overview) lets your business keep another payment channel on the plan so the renewal can still clear.


**Why do e-wallet payments fail for high-value orders?**


[Each payment channel has a minimum and maximum amount per transaction](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) , and an order above the maximum fails with a failure code showing that the payment amount limit was exceeded. Through


**Xendit** , for example, GrabPay in Malaysia accepts up to MYR 1,500 per transaction and ShopeePay in Malaysia up to MYR 4,999, while FPX online banking accepts up to MYR 30,000. With this, your checkout can hide methods that cannot cover the order value and offer ones that can.


**Which payment methods can be saved as backup channels for recurring payments?**


A backup channel has to support saving the customer's payment details and charging them without the customer present, known as a


[merchant-initiated transaction](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/cards-recurring-and-merchant-initiated-transactions) . Through


**Xendit** , this includes cards and


[a range of local payment methods](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-methods) , such as OVO and DANA in Indonesia, Maya in the Philippines, Touch 'n Go in Malaysia, and direct debit with major banks in Thailand. Offering one of these at sign-up alongside a card gives


[Xendit Subscriptions](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/subscriptions/) a second route when the first charge fails.
